  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 4 ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360 In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking. During these men's lives (and partly thanks to their efforts), \"Cold Injury\" (shangban 傷寒) replaced \"Wind illnesses\" as the new dominant class of illnesses. matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: Liu Wansu was born in northern China under Song Huizong (r. 1100-1126), the famous painter-emperor whose sumptuous reign ended when he lost half of his empire to northern invaders, the Jurchens who founded the Jin dynasty in 1115. $ ^{1} $ From his mid-twenties, Liu pored through Wang Bing's annotated version of the Basic Questions and became engrossed in the complexity of its immensely influential cosmological chapters. $ ^{2} $ To those tenacious enough to decipher them, these chapters explained the convoluted workings of the “five circulatory phases and six seasonal influences” (wuyun liuqi 五運六氣; often referred to as yunqi) as they applied to medicine. $ ^{3} $ The “five circulatory phases” were Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water, the Five Agents familiar to those who have studied any aspect of Chinese thought. The six types of climatic Qi were Wind 風, Heat 熱, Dampness 濕, Fire 火 (or Summer Heat 署), Dryness 燥, and Cold 寒.
